Ken Fisher has spent more than four decades betting that big, globally dominant companies keep winning, and his latest filing shows he still believes it. Fisher Asset Management, the firm behind Fisher Investments, reported a 13F portfolio worth about $348.3 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up from roughly $335.8 billion three months earlier. The filing backs that optimism. Across the firm's 10 largest stock positions, Fisher added shares to every one in the third quarter. Seven of those 10 are tech, cloud or chip companies, led by the AI chip giant now dealing with the sudden exit of its founder-CEO. That concentration is a bet that AI spending, cloud growth and chip demand still have years to run. Our list ranks the 10 stocks with the largest share of Fisher Asset Management's 13F portfolio for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, by the value of the fund's stake, leaving out options and ETFs. TSMC earned its spot with a stake worth $8.64 billion, or 2.48% of the portfolio. The fund held about 18.93 million shares, nearly unchanged from the prior quarter. TSMC manufactures the advanced chips that power most of the AI build-out, which makes it a way to own the boom without picking which chip designer wins. That neutrality matters more now that the leading AI chipmaker is searching for a new CEO. Demand is still accelerating. On November 10, TSMC reported October revenue of about NT$586.9 billion, up 59.7% year over year and 14.7% from September. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached about NT$4.49 trillion, up 43.3% from a year earlier. Geography, alongside cost, poses the risks that generate the bearish concerns in the market. TSMC's most advanced production is concentrated in Taiwan, and building new fabs in the U.S. and elsewhere is expensive. Also, if there were to be any slowdown in AI orders, it would hit its fastest-growing lines first. Fisher's share count was nearly unchanged in the quarter, up about 0.4%, suggesting he is content to hold rather than chase. How much that record demand is costing TSMC to meet is a fair question, and one we examined in detail. title: TSM Stock: TSMC, Samsung Halt Some China Chip Shipments - FinanceFeeds
content: TSM stock traded 1.76% higher at $369.00 in thin premarket dealings at 6:40 a.m. ET on 19 November, according to TradingView, after the Financial Times reported that TSMC and Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers. The ADR closed at $362.62 on 18 November, up 0.81%, and swung on both sides of that level in overnight trading. The two chipmakers told Chinese customers in recent days that they will halt certain processors while they apply for US Commerce Department licenses, the FT reported, citing multiple people briefed on the matter. Their pause follows a rule the Commerce Department released on 16 November, the day before Nvidia’s $115.8 billion quarter. TSM stock lost 11.04% over five sessions and 14% over a month, though it remains up 16.23% this year, TradingView data show. TSMC’s market value stood at about $1.71 trillion. TSMC did not respond to the FT’s request for comment, and Samsung declined to comment. TSM stock had already fallen through mid-November as AI shares sold off around Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia. The interim final rule, “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,” takes effect on publication in the Federal Register, scheduled for 19 November, according to Gibson Dunn. It requires a license when a foundry or packaging company ships an advanced logic chip from a designer that is not approved or authorized, to any destination. The rule also removes the transistor-count attestation for designers headquartered in China and other Country Group D:5 destinations, Ashurst said. Foundries must presume that chips at 16/14nm or below are controlled. Shipments already en route may proceed if completed within 30 days. Chinese designers had placed orders through independent packaging and testing companies that verified designs fell outside US controls, the FT reported. Under the rule, they can no longer use that route. TSM stock traded 1.76% higher in thin premarket dealings after the FT report, so the pause has not yet shown up as a lasting hit to the shares. The rule scraps exemptions that let chipmakers show a design served non-AI uses such as smartphones, the FT reported. A lawyer briefed on the matter told the FT that TSMC and Samsung now need licenses for consumer chips made on advanced processes. TSMC makes smartphone chips for Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo. An industry insider told the FT that Commerce would likely grant licenses for smartphone chips, though the wait would cause significant manufacturing delays. Smartphones made up 21% of TSMC’s third-quarter revenue and high-performance computing 68%, The Next Web reported. TSMC guided fourth-quarter revenue to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, according to its third-quarter results. Chief executive C.C. Wei said the company was “being prudent in our business planning going into 2027.” Samsung’s Chinese customers include Baidu’s AI data center unit Kunlun and TikTok owner ByteDance, the FT reported. Both have sought to diversify supply as Nvidia processors run short in China. On 18 November, Shanghai Securities News called a rumor of a Samsung foundry crackdown inaccurate, BigGo Finance reported. Chinese AI chip stocks including Moore Threads and MetaX fell on 19 November. The rule also adds license requirements for data centers serving more than 12 million aggregate TPP to covered Chinese companies, roughly 750 Nvidia H100s. Nvidia’s outlook already assumes no China data center compute revenue. That leaves TSM stock exposed mainly through customers that design chips for Chinese buyers, as investors weigh AI data center spending and a December Fed hike that futures priced near 84% after the October meeting and Polymarket at 85.5% after October’s CPI. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) stock looks too cheap for its growth outlook. The leading semiconductor foundry has fallen with the wider artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Shares are down roughly 26% since hitting an early-October peak of $487, pulled down by a semiconductor sell-off triggered by leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA) and fresh U.S. export curbs. On the company's third-quarter earnings call in October, CEO C.C. Wei said, "demand for our leading-edge technologies continues to be extremely robust." The company's October 2026 revenue also grew 59.7% year-over-year. While AI spending could disappoint, and China restrictions carry real consequences, TSMC's customers still need more advanced manufacturing capacity than it can supply. At about 15.38x next year's earnings, I think the sell-off offers an attractive entry point. I therefore rate TSM stock a Buy. Get 75% Off TipRanks Premium and unlock powerful investing tools to make smarter, more confident investment decisions Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks AI fears have overshadowed TSMC's position, in my view. Investors are questioning whether hyperscalers will earn adequate returns on enormous infrastructure spending. Nvidia's leadership turmoil has intensified uncertainty around its China business. The announcement from Washington earlier this week adds tougher foundry-customer checks and restrictions targeting China's remote access to advanced AI computing. Those developments can remove potential orders. Nvidia is a major customer, and a broader spending slowdown would affect TSMC. Its customer diversity doesn't protect it from an industry-wide retrenchment. Rather, it provides exposure across competing chip designs. Nvidia could lose some accelerator share while AMD (AMD) gains it. Both companies rely on TSMC for advanced manufacturing. Google (GOOGL) and Amazon's (AMZN) custom accelerators provide other routes for AI spending to reach the foundry. Broadcom's (AVGO) designs are another example. Its latest quarterly filing says TSMC produced roughly 95% of wafers supplied by its contract manufacturers during the first nine months. So changing winners among chip designers needn't mean fewer orders for TSMC. That distinction is central to my thesis. Customers can compete fiercely over AI profits while continuing to buy manufacturing services from the same supplier. TSMC's process expertise makes switching difficult. Its enormous scale also helps spread development costs across a broad customer base. Building another leading-edge factory takes years, and matching its yields is a separate challenge. I think the market is applying too much of chip designers' uncertainty to the company that manufactures their products. TSMC's October revenue strengthens the growth case after an already excellent Q3. Quarterly revenue rose 50.9% in Taiwan dollars, while net income increased 68.7%. Gross margin reached 66.4%, and 2nm contributed 8% of wafer revenue. Then last week's monthly report showed record October revenue of NT$586.9 billion (about $17.8 billion). That was up 14.7% sequentially and 59.7% year-over-year. Revenue through October increased 43.3%. Growth accelerated after Q3, using the same local-currency comparison. That's difficult to reconcile with the idea that demand is already weakening materially. Management's Q4 revenue guidance of $52.3 billion–$54.3 billion comes with 65%–67% gross margins. The steep 2nm ramp should help. More revealing, though, is the spending commitment beyond this quarter. TSMC expects $60 billion–$64 billion of capex in 2026, and management indicated that total investment over 2026–2028 should significantly exceed the previous three years. Since leading-edge capacity takes years to bring online, customers plan capacity alongside TSMC well in advance. Management has even sent teams to check U.S. data center construction and power availability. Capex doesn't guarantee future sales, but collaborative capacity planning gives these investment figures far more weight than an optimistic forecast alone. The 2nm family's annual capacity should more than double in 2027. A16 expands its high-performance computing offering, while A14 volume production is planned for 2028. Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) packaging remains another scarce capability needed to assemble advanced AI systems. Agentic workloads are increasing demand for central processing units (CPUs), alongside inference accelerators and networking chips. Smartphones also support adoption of advanced processes. Overseas expansion, including Arizona's next fab in 2027, adds capacity across more locations. So I see a manufacturing franchise expanding around several sources of demand, with customers already planning subsequent product generations. TSMC's valuation leaves room for excellent returns if earnings follow current expectations. At today's price, consensus 2026 earnings per share (EPS) of $17.50 implies 20.55x earnings. The $23.39 estimate for 2027 reduces that to 15.38x. By 2028, $29.82 of EPS implies just 12.06x. Those forecasts assume roughly 34% earnings growth next year and 27.5% afterward. This is an unusually modest price for this growth profile. The opportunity has historical context. Forward P/E fell near 12x–13x in late 2022 and roughly 15x during parts of 2023. Patient buyers eventually benefited as earnings recovered and the shares rerated. I use that comparison cautiously. Still, today's business is growing rapidly, with October revenue 59.7% higher. The technology position remains strong, and new capacity is being planned against customer demand. That makes a compressed multiple particularly interesting to me. Customer concentration and Taiwan's geopolitical risks deserve a valuation discount. Export restrictions could tighten further, and enormous capex creates financial exposure if demand slows. Overseas fabs can also pressure margins. Eventually, leading-edge supply could catch up. Still, even 16x the 2028 EPS estimate would imply roughly $477 per share before dividends. That illustrates why the return case can work without an extreme valuation. Further estimate increases would provide additional upside. Taiwan Semiconductor stock has a Strong Buy consensus on TipRanks, based on nine unanimous Buy ratings. The average price target of $563.75 implies roughly 57% upside from today's price levels. Wall Street therefore remains optimistic despite the recent deterioration in semiconductor sentiment. TSMC will feel any genuine slowdown in AI investment. Yet its latest revenue figures show customers still demanding more leading-edge capacity. It can benefit as competing chip designers expand, even as market shares shift. At about 15.38x 2027 earnings, I think that position is attractively priced. October's revenue acceleration gives me more confidence in buying the decline.
